t: #3563 Lexicographically Smallest String After Adjacent Removals — Interval DP with Wraparound Pairs
o: Removals shift characters together, so originally distant letters can pair up ("bcda" → drop "cd" → "ba" → drop → ""). The right model is a CFG: a substring reduces to empty iff it is R → RR | a·R·b for alphabet-consecutive a,b (circularly, so 'a'/'z' count). First compute del[i][j] with CYK-style DP. Then best[i][j] = the lexicographically smallest reachable string from s[i..j]: either keep s[i] (prepend to best of the rest), split into two independent reductions, or delete s[i] together with some later partner s[p] provided the stretch between them reduces to empty. Example "zdce" keeps everything since deleting "dc" only yields the larger "ze".
k: Reduction language: R → RR | a R b | ab for circularly consecutive a,b — captured by an interval DP including the wrapping production.
Any reachable result keeps some subsequence; the first kept char is s[i], or s[i] is deleted by pairing with s[p] after s[i+1..p−1] fully reduces.
best[i][j] = min( splits, s[i]+best[i+1][j], best[p+1][j] for valid pair-deletes, "" if del[i][j] ).

a.n: Approach 1: Reducibility DP + Lexicographic Interval DP
a.i: Phase 1 fills del[i][j] in O(n³) using both the split production and the a-R-b production (with circular consecutiveness: difference 1 or 25). Phase 2 fills best[i][j] by increasing length with the three transition families; if del[i][j] the answer is "" outright.
s: del[i][j] = (consec(s[i],s[j]) and (j=i+1 or del[i+1][j-1])) or exists k with del[i][k] and del[k+1][j].
best[i][j]: start with s[i]+best[i+1][j]; try all splits; for each p>i with consec(s[i],s[p]) and del[i+1][p-1], try best[p+1][j]; if del[i][j], answer "".
a.t: O(n³) string work — n = 250 gives ~15M character operations across both phases
a.sp: O(n²) — the del table and memo of strings

w: The pivotal insight is that removals make far-apart characters adjacent, so plain "contiguous-interval reducibility" fails ("bcda" proves it) — you need the a·R·b production. The second DP's case analysis (keep first char / pair-delete it with a later partner) is complete because a kept first character never interacts with reductions to its right. Validate on all three examples, especially "zdce", where doing nothing wins. Follow-up: count reachable strings, or return the minimum-length result instead of the lexicographically smallest.
